newsitem.title: USA: Proposed US tax cuts are small, prudent - Rubin.
newsitem.headline: Proposed US tax cuts are small, prudent - Rubin.

text.p: Tax-cut proposals in a budget-balancing pact reached between Congress and the Clinton administration are relatively very small and present no threat to progress in shrinking the deficit, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Tuesday.
"...We can afford it in the shorter run and it is not going to undo the very real progress we've made in deficit reduction in the longer run," Rubin told reporters at a Treasury briefing.
The tax-cut package negotiated late Monday is estimated to amount to more than $90 billion over five years.

In response to questions, Rubin said he considered it a good tax bill, though it includes reductions in capital gains taxes that he said he preferred were not in it. "Part of that is because we started with a tax cut we could afford rather than one that was out-sized," Rubin added."
The package must still be voted on by Congress. Final figures were not yet available on Tuesday in published form for the costs of many of the tax cuts in the agreement.
Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers described the tax cuts as "a fiscally responsible dividend on the progress that we've made in deficit reduction."
But Summers insisted "it's nothing like 1981" when the former Reagan administration introduced a much more sweeping tax-reduction effort.

The 1981 tax cuts amounted to about 2 percent of total national output in the later years of the tax-reducing effort, whereas the current package is only about three-tenths of one percentage point of the U.S. Gross Domestic Product, he added.

"This is a good, fiscally prudent package," Rubin said, adding that the costs of a $500-per-child tax credit, tax breaks for higher education and other measures amounted to only "minute percentages of GDP."

Though final figures still were being worked out, Rubin estimated that the tax breaks for education costs would cost Treasury roughly $35 billion in lost tax income over five years and that the child tax credit would cost about $80 billion.
"In terms of equity, certainly by far the largest part...of the tax cut will be going to middle-income people, which is where I think it should go," Rubin said.

Rubin said the child tax credit would specially benefit Americans in lower-income levels and added that winning acceptance for it had been a primary goal of the Clinton administration "that was accomplished in its fullness."
